claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia are recently diverged species with differential diet choice.
source: We have addressed this question by analyzing Drosophila simulans and sechellia, recently diverged species with differential diet choice.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a premise of the study.

claim: D. sechellia larvae, specialized to a nutrient scarce diet, did not survive on sugar-rich conditions.
source: D. sechellia larvae, specialized to a nutrient scarce diet, did not survive on sugar-rich conditions, while the generalist species D. simulans was sugar tolerant.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: D. simulans was sugar tolerant.
source: D. sechellia larvae, specialized to a nutrient scarce diet, did not survive on sugar-rich conditions, while the generalist species D. simulans was sugar tolerant.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sugar tolerance in D. simulans was a tradeoff for performance on low-energy diet.
source: Sugar tolerance in D. simulans was a tradeoff for performance on low-energy diet and was associated with global reprogramming of metabolic gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sugar tolerance was associated with global reprogramming of metabolic gene expression.
source: Sugar tolerance in D. simulans was a tradeoff for performance on low-energy diet and was associated with global reprogramming of metabolic gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Hybridization and phenotype-based introgression revealed the genomic regions of D. simulans that were sufficient for sugar tolerance.
source: Hybridization and phenotype-based introgression revealed the genomic regions of D. simulans that were sufficient for sugar tolerance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: The genomic regions sufficient for sugar tolerance included genes involved in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis.
source: These regions included genes that are involved in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis and intracellular signaling, such as PPP1R15/Gadd34 and SERCA, which contributed to sugar tolerance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The genomic regions sufficient for sugar tolerance included genes involved in intracellular signaling, such as PPP1R15/Gadd34 and SERCA.
source: These regions included genes that are involved in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis and intracellular signaling, such as PPP1R15/Gadd34 and SERCA, which contributed to sugar tolerance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PPP1R15/Gadd34 and SERCA contributed to sugar tolerance.
source: These regions included genes that are involved in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis and intracellular signaling, such as PPP1R15/Gadd34 and SERCA, which contributed to sugar tolerance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Genomic variation affecting genes involved in global metabolic control defines the optimal range for dietary macronutrient composition.
source: In conclusion, genomic variation affecting genes involved in global metabolic control defines the optimal range for dietary macronutrient composition.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: The balance between nutrients has significant effects on development, reproduction and longevity.
source: Animals require macronutrients to sustain growth, reproduction and repair over their lifetimes and the balance between nutrients has been shown to have significant effects on development, reproduction and longevity (Raubenheimer and Simpson, 1997; Lee et al., 2008; Arganda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most animals consume a variety of different foods to meet their nutritional needs.
source: Most animals consume a variety of different foods to meet their nutritional needs (Raubenheimer and Simpson, 1997; Lee et al., 2008) and even closely related species make highly distinct diet choices (Tinker et al., 2008; Goldman-Huertas et al., 2015; Salinas-Ramos et al., 2015; Costello et al., 2016; Han et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Even closely related species make highly distinct diet choices.
source: Most animals consume a variety of different foods to meet their nutritional needs (Raubenheimer and Simpson, 1997; Lee et al., 2008) and even closely related species make highly distinct diet choices (Tinker et al., 2008; Goldman-Huertas et al., 2015; Salinas-Ramos et al., 2015; Costello et al., 2016; Han et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some closely related species are distinguished by variation in morphological structures that are specialized for obtaining nutrients from unique resources.
source: Some closely related species are distinguished by variation in morphological structures that are specialized for obtaining nutrients from unique resources (trophic morphology) (Malinsky et al., 2015; Parsons et al., 2016; Santana and Cheung, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Darwin's finches are the classic example of species that are differentiated in part by interspecific competition and specialization on an under-used food type.
source: Darwin's finches are the classic example of species that are differentiated in part by interspecific competition and specialization on an under-used food type (De León et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Darwin's finches are considered 'imperfect dietary generalists'.
source: Darwin's finches are considered 'imperfect dietary generalists' (De León et al., 2014) having similar preferred diets that overlap among species but specialize on a unique food when the preferred diet is limiting.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Metabolic phenotypes and diet tolerance vary with ecological diversification within and between species.
source: Metabolic phenotypes and diet tolerance is observed to vary with ecological diversification within and between species (Matzkin et al., 2009; Reed et al., 2010; Matzkin et al., 2011), and these phenotypic changes correlate with changes in gene expression (Nazario-Yepiz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phenotypic changes in metabolic phenotypes correlate with changes in gene expression.
source: Metabolic phenotypes and diet tolerance is observed to vary with ecological diversification within and between species (Matzkin et al., 2009; Reed et al., 2010; Matzkin et al., 2011), and these phenotypic changes correlate with changes in gene expression (Nazario-Yepiz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Flexibility in the usage of metabolic pathways allows animals to accommodate changes in food nutrient content and availability.
source: Flexibility in the usage of metabolic pathways allows animals to accommodate changes in food nutrient content and availability.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Systemic nutrient levels are actively monitored by nutrient-sensing pathways composed of intra- and intercellular signaling pathways and gene regulatory networks.
source: At the level of the organism, systemic nutrient levels are actively monitored by the so-called nutrient-sensing pathways composed of intra- and intercellular signaling pathways and gene regulatory networks, which ultimately control the activity of metabolic pathways (Mattila and Hietakangas, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nutrient-sensing pathways ultimately control the activity of metabolic pathways.
source: At the level of the organism, systemic nutrient levels are actively monitored by the so-called nutrient-sensing pathways composed of intra- and intercellular signaling pathways and gene regulatory networks, which ultimately control the activity of metabolic pathways (Mattila and Hietakangas, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There are specific nutrient-sensing mechanisms for each type of macronutrient.
source: There are specific nutrient-sensing mechanisms for each type of macronutrient.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge, followed by specific examples.

claim: Protein kinases mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and GCN2 respond to changes in amino acid availability.
source: For example, protein kinases mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and GCN2 respond to changes in amino acid availability (Efeyan et al., 2015), while the transcription factor complex Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx is activated in response to sugars (Havula and Hietakangas, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The transcription factor complex Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx is activated in response to sugars.
source: For example, protein kinases mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and GCN2 respond to changes in amino acid availability (Efeyan et al., 2015), while the transcription factor complex Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx is activated in response to sugars (Havula and Hietakangas, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult mutants of 4EBP are indistinguishable from controls when fed a protein-rich diet, but are sensitive to amino acid starvation.
source: Adult mutants of 4EBP, a target of mTORC1, are indistinguishable from controls when fed a protein-rich diet, but are sensitive to amino acid starvation (Teleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: mlx mutant larvae have impaired function of the sugar sensor Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx and grow normally when fed a low sugar diet.
source: On the other hand, mlx mutant larvae have impaired function of the sugar sensor Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx and grow normally when fed a low sugar diet (LSD), but are intolerant of high-sugar diet (HSD) (Havula et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: mlx mutant larvae are intolerant of high-sugar diet (HSD).
source: On the other hand, mlx mutant larvae have impaired function of the sugar sensor Mondo/ChREBP-Mlx and grow normally when fed a low sugar diet (LSD), but are intolerant of high-sugar diet (HSD) (Havula et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mlx null mutants exhibit impaired growth, increased larval development time and reduced larvae to pupae survival when the high dietary sugar concentration is within the range available from natural food sources.
source: The mlx null mutants exhibit impaired growth, increased larval development time and reduced larvae to pupae survival when the high dietary sugar concentration is within the range available from natural food sources (Havula et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nutrient-sensing pathways define the tolerated lower and upper limits of nutrient intake.
source: Thus, nutrient-sensing pathways define the tolerated lower and upper limits of nutrient intake.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the examples of 4EBP and mlx mutants.

claim: The limits for each nutrient depend on the availability of other nutrients.
source: These limits for each nutrient will further depend on the availability of other nutrients.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the concept of macronutrient interactions.

claim: In nature, D. simulans larvae consume a range of decaying fruits that may contain high levels of sugars.
source: In nature, D. simulans larvae consume a range of decaying fruits that may contain high levels of sugars, whereas D. sechellia larvae grow on the unripe fruits of Morinda citrifolia, which has a low-sugar content (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: D. sechellia larvae grow on the unripe fruits of Morinda citrifolia, which has a low-sugar content.
source: In nature, D. simulans larvae consume a range of decaying fruits that may contain high levels of sugars, whereas D. sechellia larvae grow on the unripe fruits of Morinda citrifolia, which has a low-sugar content (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia occur together on islands of the Seychelles archipelago.
source: The two species occur together on islands of the Seychelles archipelago; however, D. sechellia adults and larvae are found infrequently on fruits other than that of Morinda (R'Kha et al., 1991; Matute and Ayroles, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D. sechellia adults and larvae are found infrequently on fruits other than that of Morinda.
source: The two species occur together on islands of the Seychelles archipelago; however, D. sechellia adults and larvae are found infrequently on fruits other than that of Morinda (R'Kha et al., 1991; Matute and Ayroles, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia show strong dietary differentiation yet they are closely related and can form fertile female F1 hybrids.
source: D. simulans and D. sechellia show strong dietary differentiation yet they are closely related and can form fertile female F1 hybrids (Lachaise et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: D. simulans larvae displayed rapid development and high larval survival on diets up to and including 20% sugar.
source: D. simulans larvae displayed rapid development and high larval survival on diets up to and including 20% sugar.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: D. sechellia larvae displayed a more restricted space, with slowed development and reduced survival on high-protein diets containing >10% sugar.
source: In contrast, D. sechellia larvae displayed a more restricted space, with slowed development and reduced survival on high-protein diets containing >10% sugar and complete lethality on diet composed of 20% sucrose/20% yeast (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: D. sechellia larvae showed complete lethality on diet composed of 20% sucrose/20% yeast.
source: In contrast, D. sechellia larvae displayed a more restricted space, with slowed development and reduced survival on high-protein diets containing >10% sugar and complete lethality on diet composed of 20% sucrose/20% yeast (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: For D. sechellia larvae, dietary sucrose concentration showed significant (p < 0.001) positive correlation with lengthened development time.
source: For D. sechellia larvae, dietary sucrose concentration showed significant (p < 0.001) positive correlation with lengthened development time and significant (p < 0.001) negative correlation with survival, but such correlations were not observed for D. simulans larvae (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: For D. sechellia larvae, dietary sucrose concentration showed significant (p < 0.001) negative correlation with survival.
source: For D. sechellia larvae, dietary sucrose concentration showed significant (p < 0.001) positive correlation with lengthened development time and significant (p < 0.001) negative correlation with survival, but such correlations were not observed for D. simulans larvae (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Such correlations between dietary sucrose and development time/survival were not observed for D. simulans larvae.
source: For D. sechellia larvae, dietary sucrose concentration showed significant (p < 0.001) positive correlation with lengthened development time and significant (p < 0.001) negative correlation with survival, but such correlations were not observed for D. simulans larvae (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: For both species, larval development time was negatively correlated and survival was positively correlated with dietary yeast concentration.
source: For both species, larval development time was negatively correlated and survival was positively correlated with dietary yeast concentration; however, the correlation was weaker for D. sechellia than for D. simulans (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The correlation between dietary yeast concentration and development time/survival was weaker for D. sechellia than for D. simulans.
source: For both species, larval development time was negatively correlated and survival was positively correlated with dietary yeast concentration; however, the correlation was weaker for D. sechellia than for D. simulans (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: ANOVA showed no significant effect of species (F(1, 12) = 0.06, p = 0.81), sugar concentration (F(1, 12) = 0.42, p = 0.53), or their interaction (F(1,12) = 4.47, p = 0.06) on feeding behavior.
source: ANOVA showed no significant effect of species (F(1, 12) = 0.06, p = 0.81), sugar concentration (F(1, 12) = 0.42, p = 0.53), or their interaction (F(1,12) = 4.47, p = 0.06) on feeding behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of the Pupind of D. simulans and sechellia confirmed the poor performance of sechellia on high-sugar diets.
source: Analysis of the Pupind of D. simulans and sechellia confirmed the poor performance of sechellia on high-sugar diets (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: A full generalized linear model (glm) showed significant effects of genotype, percent sugar, percent yeast, and all interactions of the main effects on larval development time, larval survival, and Pupind.
source: We further analyzed our data by using a full generalized linear model (glm), which showed significant effects of genotype, percent sugar, percent yeast, and all interactions of the main effects on larval development time, larval survival, and Pupind (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: The effect of yeast on Pupind was stronger for D. simulans than for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.94 and 0.33, respectively).
source: However, while the effect of yeast on Pupind was stronger for D. simulans than for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.94 and 0.33, respectively), the effect of sugar on Pupind was substantially stronger for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.01 and 0.35 for D. simulans and D. sechellia, respectively) (Table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: The effect of sugar on Pupind was substantially stronger for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.01 and 0.35 for D. simulans and D. sechellia, respectively).
source: However, while the effect of yeast on Pupind was stronger for D. simulans than for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.94 and 0.33, respectively), the effect of sugar on Pupind was substantially stronger for D. sechellia (ω2 = 0.01 and 0.35 for D. simulans and D. sechellia, respectively) (Table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia are closely related, having diverged from a common ancestor roughly 0.4 million years ago.
source: D. simulans and D. sechellia are closely related, having diverged from a common ancestor roughly 0.4 million years ago (Kliman et al., 2000), and hybrid females from the cross, D. sechellia male × D. simulans female, are fertile (Lachaise et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hybrid females from the cross, D. sechellia male × D. simulans female, are fertile.
source: D. simulans and D. sechellia are closely related, having diverged from a common ancestor roughly 0.4 million years ago (Kliman et al., 2000), and hybrid females from the cross, D. sechellia male × D. simulans female, are fertile (Lachaise et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A clear rescue of sugar tolerant larval development and survival was observed in the F1 hybrid.
source: We observed a clear rescue of sugar tolerant larval development and survival in the F1 hybrid (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sugar intolerance phenotype of D. sechellia may be caused by altered function of genes underlying sugar tolerance.
source: This implied that the sugar intolerance phenotype of D. sechellia may be caused by altered function of genes underlying sugar tolerance
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue of sugar tolerance in F1 hybrids.

claim: After 10 generations of backcrossing with selection, tolerance of an HSD (20% yeast/20% sugar) in the backcross larvae was equal to that of D. simulans.
source: After 10 generations of backcrossing with selection, we observed that tolerance of an HSD (20% yeast/20% sugar) in the backcross larvae was equal to that of D. simulans (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A control fly line that was backcrossed in the same manner, but not selected on a high-sugar diet, showed only minimal tolerance for HSD.
source: A control fly line that was backcrossed in the same manner, but not selected on a high-sugar diet, showed only minimal tolerance for HSD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mitochondrial genomes of the selected and control lines are the same.
source: Since the introgression was performed by repeated backcrossing of D. sechellia males with the hybrid line (maternally D. simulans), the mitochondrial genomes of the selected and control lines are the same.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crossing scheme used in the introgression experiment.

claim: The observed phenotypic differences are due to the nuclear genome.
source: Therefore, the observed phenotypic differences are due to the nuclear genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that mitochondrial genomes are the same in selected and control lines.

claim: The sugar intolerant D. sechellia and no-selection control lines were less efficient in clearing glucose from circulation after challenge with high-sugar diet.
source: Metabolic analysis of the parental and introgressed lines revealed that the sugar intolerant D. sechellia and no-selection control lines were less efficient in clearing glucose from circulation after challenge with high-sugar diet (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pathways controlling energy metabolism or their response toward high-sugar diet are affected by the genomic regions underlying sugar tolerance.
source: This suggests that the pathways controlling energy metabolism or their response toward high-sugar diet are affected by the genomic regions underlying sugar tolerance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the glucose clearance data.

claim: The gene expression profile of the sugar-selected hybrid had high similarity with that of D. simulans.
source: Global comparison of the gene expression by sample clustering revealed striking association between expression profiles and sugar tolerance. The gene expression profile of the sugar-selected hybrid had high similarity with that of D. simulans, while the sugar intolerant control hybrid clustered close to D. sechellia (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sugar intolerant control hybrid clustered close to D. sechellia.
source: Global comparison of the gene expression by sample clustering revealed striking association between expression profiles and sugar tolerance. The gene expression profile of the sugar-selected hybrid had high similarity with that of D. simulans, while the sugar intolerant control hybrid clustered close to D. sechellia (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The genetic factors underlying the differences in sugar tolerance explain the majority of the differential gene expression between the parental species.
source: This implies, surprisingly, that the genetic factors underlying the differences in sugar tolerance explain the majority of the differential gene expression between the parental species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering of gene expression profiles.

claim: Genes with reduced expression in both sugar intolerant lines displayed significant (p < 0.05) enrichment in functional categories related to mitochondrial ribosome, detoxification (e.g. cytochrome P450 and glutathione metabolism), growth control (ribosome biogenesis), carbohydrate metabolism (starch and sucrose metabolism) as well as several categories related to amino acid metabolism.
source: Genes with reduced expression in both sugar intolerant lines displayed significant (p < 0.05) enrichment in functional categories related to mitochondrial ribosome, detoxification (e.g. cytochrome P450 and glutathione metabolism), growth control (ribosome biogenesis), carbohydrate metabolism (starch and sucrose metabolism) as well as several categories related to amino acid metabolism (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genes with high expression in sugar intolerant lines displayed overrepresentation of proteolysis and lysosome.
source: On the other hand, genes with high expression in sugar intolerant lines displayed overrepresentation of proteolysis and lysosome (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mlx1 null mutant larvae, lacking functional sugar sensing by Mondo-Mlx, display strong sugar intolerance, similar to D. sechellia.
source: We have earlier observed that the mlx1 null mutant larvae, lacking functional sugar sensing by Mondo-Mlx, display strong sugar intolerance, similar to D. sechellia (Havula et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There was significant similarity between the gene expression profiles of the sugar intolerant genotypes and mlx1 mutants.
source: There was significant similarity between the gene expression profiles of the sugar intolerant genotypes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 30% (174/587; p = 1.2×10−69) of the genes downregulated in mlx1 mutants displayed reduced expression in D. sechellia and the control hybrid line.
source: For example, 30% (174/587; p = 1.2×10−69) of the genes downregulated in mlx1 mutants displayed reduced expression in D. sechellia and the control hybrid line (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Global comparison of all genes with similar gene expression differences in tolerant and intolerant lines revealed a high degree of similarity in the gene expression patterns.
source: Global comparison of all genes with similar gene expression differences in tolerant and intolerant lines revealed a high degree of similarity in the gene expression patterns (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overlapping gene sets included several genes that were upregulated upon sugar feeding in sugar tolerant genotypes, but the activation was either absent or reduced in the sugar intolerant genotypes.
source: These overlapping gene sets included several genes that were upregulated upon sugar feeding in sugar tolerant genotypes, but the activation was either absent or reduced in the sugar intolerant genotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The transcription factor sugarbabe and Phosphoserine phosphatase astray are essential for sugar tolerance.
source: These include, for example the transcription factor sugarbabe and Phosphoserine phosphatase astray (Figure 4C,D), which we have earlier shown to be essential for sugar tolerance (Mattila et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: SNP analysis showed three small and one large region of D. simulans SNPs on chromosome arm 2R.
source: SNP analysis showed three small and one large region of D. simulans SNPs on chromosome arm 2R, while all other regions of the genome showed an almost completely D. sechellia SNP signature (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: All other regions of the genome showed an almost completely D. sechellia SNP signature.
source: SNP analysis showed three small and one large region of D. simulans SNPs on chromosome arm 2R, while all other regions of the genome showed an almost completely D. sechellia SNP signature (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Locations of the introgressions relative to nucleotide positions on the D. melanogaster chromosome arm 2R were from approximately 5,758,067 to 6,085,625 (spanning 25 annotated D. melanogaster genes); from 6,600,044 to 6,810,530 (spanning 35 annotated genes); and 21,774,876 to 24,092,079 (spanning 312 annotated genes).
source: Locations of the introgressions relative to nucleotide positions on the D. melanogaster chromosome arm 2R were from approximately 5,758,067 to 6,085,625 (spanning 25 annotated D. melanogaster genes); from 6,600,044 to 6,810,530 (spanning 35 annotated genes); and 21,774,876 to 24,092,079 (spanning 312 annotated genes) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Majority of the introgressed genes showed no significant changes in gene expression.
source: Majority of the introgressed genes showed no significant changes in gene expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In total, 40 introgressed genes were significantly (p < 0.05) downregulated in the intolerant lines.
source: In total, 40 introgressed genes were significantly (p < 0.05) downregulated in the intolerant lines, while 24 displayed elevated expression associated with sugar intolerance (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 24 introgressed genes displayed elevated expression associated with sugar intolerance.
source: In total, 40 introgressed genes were significantly (p < 0.05) downregulated in the intolerant lines, while 24 displayed elevated expression associated with sugar intolerance (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The global gene expression differences between sugar tolerant and intolerant lines are likely due to a small number of loci, which control the expression of a large number of downstream genes.
source: This suggests that the global gene expression differences between sugar tolerant and intolerant lines are likely due to a small number of loci, which control the expression of a large number of downstream genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that most introgressed genes show no expression changes.

claim: D. melanogaster is a dietary generalist and close relative of D. simulans and sechellia with sugar tolerance similar to that of D. simulans.
source: To identify genes from the introgressed chromosome 2R regions that were potentially responsible for the sugar tolerance phenotype, we utilized the genetic toolkit of D. melanogaster, a dietary generalist and close relative of D. simulans and sechellia with sugar tolerance similar to that of D. simulans (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three of the identified sugar tolerance genes, mRpL43, CG4882 and bonsai encode components of the mitochondrial ribosome.
source: Interestingly, three of the identified sugar tolerance genes, mRpL43, CG4882 and bonsai encode components of the mitochondrial ribosome (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: mRpL43, CG4882 and bonsai displayed reduced expression in sugar intolerant genotypes.
source: Furthermore, all of them displayed reduced expression in sugar intolerant genotypes (Figure 6D–F), implying that reduced capacity mitochondrial protein biosynthesis contributes to the sugar intolerance phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: Reduced capacity mitochondrial protein biosynthesis contributes to the sugar intolerance phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, all of them displayed reduced expression in sugar intolerant genotypes (Figure 6D–F), implying that reduced capacity mitochondrial protein biosynthesis contributes to the sugar intolerance phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that mitochondrial ribosome genes are downregulated in sugar intolerant lines.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA), Protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 15 (PPP1R15, Gadd34), or Phosphotidylinositol 3 kinase 59F (Pi3K59F) led to strongly impaired larval growth on high-sugar diet, with only a few larvae surviving to pupae.
source: RNAi knockdown of Sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA), Protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 15 (PPP1R15, Gadd34), or Phosphotidylinositol 3 kinase 59F (Pi3K59F) led to strongly impaired larval growth on high-sugar diet, with only a few larvae surviving to pupae (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7A–C.

source: Our study represents evidence for rapid (~0.4 MY) evolution of macronutrient space in a multicellular animal.

source: Evolution of metabolism is known to occur through multiple mechanisms, such as nonsynonymous coding region mutation, copy number variation or mutation of regulatory regions of a gene encoding a metabolic enzyme (Wagner, 2012).
